speaker: Fedor
text: Hello, we are Group 11: Alexandre, Nico, and I am Fedor. Our project is called Crowdfund Compass. On Kickstarter, a campaign that misses its goal gets nothing. So we built a check that a team can run before it launches. The app is live, and the link is on this slide.

speaker: Fedor
text: Let us start with the problem. Kickstarter is all or nothing. If a campaign asks for ten thousand dollars and collects nine thousand, the team receives zero. Kickstarter's own numbers say that only 43 percent of all campaigns ever launched reached their goal. Most founders set their goal, their launch date and their pitch by gut feeling. Now think of a startup coach, for example at Startup at HSG. The coach has many teams that want to launch, and only a few hours. Today the coach cannot see which plans are at risk. So the hours may go to the teams that ask first, rather than to the teams that need help the most.

speaker: Fedor
text: So what decision do we support? Before launch, every campaign gets one of three verdicts. Launch means the plan is not among the riskiest, and no single change would add much. It is not a promise. Adjust means there is one named change that is linked to clearly better odds. Coach first means the plan is among the riskiest, and the team should talk to a coach before it goes live. Our main user is the coach. The second user is the founder, who checks one plan. Our question is this: which campaigns should a coach see first, and for each campaign, which change is linked to the biggest rise in its odds? One honest note. Funding on Kickstarter is a market test. It does not prove that a company will survive. Let me show you what the coach sees.

speaker: Fedor
text: Here is the Coach view of our app, with an example group of six planned campaigns. The coach uploads one file with all the teams, and the app ranks them from riskiest to safest. The coach has time for two teams, so the slider is at 30 percent, and a line marks where that capacity ends. The two teams above the line get a coaching slot. Here, that is BudgetBuddy, a money app, and Voices of the Rhine, a documentary. For BudgetBuddy, the conversation is whether Kickstarter is the right route at all. For Voices of the Rhine, it is a concrete next step: a pre-launch page. Each row also shows the team's own verdict, its chance range, and the one change linked to the biggest gain. The verdict does not depend on the slider. Moving it only changes who gets a slot. So how did we build this? Alexandre.

speaker: Alex
text: Thank you, Fedor. In the first feedback session we were told: find more data, and use many more inputs. This slide is our answer. The usual public Kickstarter file gives you about six things that are known before launch, such as the category, the goal and the country. We went to the source instead. A company called Web Robots saves public Kickstarter listings. We combined 24 of these snapshots, from 2016 to 2026. That gave us 489,000 campaigns. 430,000 of them have a final outcome, funded or failed. For the final model we use about 44,000 recent campaigns, launched in 2023 and 2024, and we test it on 39,500 campaigns launched after that. The new data adds what the small file does not have: the title and the short pitch text, the earlier campaigns of the same creator, the video, the pre-launch page, and the preparation time.

speaker: Alex
text: But when we checked the data, we found a serious problem. Kickstarter hides most campaigns that failed. They do not appear in the public lists that we collected. So they are missing from our data. We measured how many. Kickstarter publishes official totals. When we compare, we have about 85 percent of all funded campaigns, but only 42 percent of all failed ones. One example makes it concrete. Kickstarter reported that 80 percent of tabletop game campaigns in 2024 were funded. In our data, it looks like 94 percent. If we had ignored this, our app would tell almost every founder that things look great. So this finding shaped everything that follows. We did three things about it. First, we judge the model inside each category, because we assume that inside a category the missing data affects campaigns in a similar way. We cannot fully check that assumption. Second, we show chances as a range, not as one exact number. Third, we give coaching slots by rank, not by a percentage.

speaker: Alex
text: A model must not see the answer. So we do not use anything that is a result of the campaign, like pledges or backers. For inputs based on history, we only use campaigns that ended before the launch, and we checked 695 campaigns with separate code. And we found one hidden leak ourselves. The video field is only filled for campaigns that Kickstarter listed recently, and that depends on whether the campaign succeeded. A model can learn this pattern instead of learning about the campaign. Look at the numbers. On old data, the score goes up from 0.90 to 0.92 with the leak. It looks like an improvement. On new data, the same model gets worse. So we use video and pre-launch page only where they are known for every campaign.

speaker: Alex
text: Now the results. Our tool will be used on future campaigns, so we test on the future. We train on campaigns from 2023 and 2024, and we test once on campaigns from 2025. Our main measure is called AUC. Take one funded and one failed campaign from the same category. How often does the model give the funded one the higher score? 0.5 is guessing. 1 is perfect. Our final model, XGBoost, a method from this course, reaches 0.86, and 0.87 on the first half of 2026. In plain accuracy, it is right for 85 percent of campaigns, against 71 percent if you always say funded. What made the difference? Not the algorithm: logistic regression is just as good. And not more history: all years of data did no better than the two most recent years. What helped was more inputs. With only the six usual inputs, the same model reaches 0.75. Our 32 inputs, all known before launch, lift it to 0.86.

speaker: Alex
text: A coach wants a percentage. Can we trust ours? The chart shows the answer for our data. On the horizontal axis is the chance the model predicts. On the vertical axis is how many of these campaigns were really funded. After a small correction, called calibration, the green line stays close to the dashed line. When the model says 70 percent, about 70 in 100 were funded. But remember, our data misses many failed campaigns. So the real chance is lower than what our data shows. That is why the app shows a range. One estimate comes from our data. The other is adjusted to Kickstarter's official rate for the category, and it is almost always the lower one. And the middle estimate lies halfway between the two. We could check this middle estimate on only one public number. For tabletop games in 2024, Kickstarter says 80 percent were funded. Our middle estimate is 78 percent. It is only one check, so we stay careful. The ranking of plans is solid. The exact percentage is rough. That is why the coaching slots are given by rank. Back to Fedor.

speaker: Fedor
text: So does the ranking help a coach? Imagine 100 planned campaigns and coaching slots for 30 of them. With our ranking, those 30 slots reach about 29 teams that will fail. With the best simple rule, picking the subcategories with the lowest funding rates, they reach about 25. That is four more struggling teams reached with the same hours. In shares, that is 51 against 45 percent of all failures, and the maximum possible is 54. We tested this on 2025 campaigns, re-weighted to Kickstarter's real mix. About 95 percent of the teams that got a slot failed. We then repeated the test on campaigns from the first half of 2026, with every setting fixed in advance. We had already seen some 2026 results, so it is not a fully blind test, but the result was the same: 51 against 45 percent. One honest limit: this measures which teams get flagged, not how much coaching helps them. And a new group of teams may differ. Nico.

speaker: Nico
text: Thank you. Before the app, one honest finding. We asked the model which inputs drive its result. The type of product explains about a third of the model's explanation. The track record of the founder explains about a quarter. The things a founder can still change before launch, the goal, the timing, the presentation and the pitch, explain 43 percent together. So less than half of the model's explanation comes from things a founder can change. The app says this openly. In the model, the changes linked to the biggest gains are a pre-launch page and more preparation time. But these stand for real groundwork, like building an audience. Our data cannot tell whether opening a page shortly before launch would help. And for about a third of campaigns, no single change adds even 2 points in the model.

speaker: Nico
text: Now the founder's side. This is the check-up for one campaign: a board game by a first-time founder who asks for 15,000 dollars. The founder fills in four short steps: what they make, money and timing, preparation, and their track record. The result appears at once. The verdict is Adjust. The chance is a range from 23 to 60 percent, with a middle estimate of 40 percent, and each end says where it comes from. The best next step is a pre-launch page. Campaigns that did this were funded more often, and the middle estimate rises from 40 to 63 percent. Below, four bars show where the plan is strong or weak. Four more pages help: a goal optimizer, similar past campaigns, Kickstarter's official benchmarks, and a page that explains the method and its limits.

speaker: Nico
text: To finish, the limits. We cannot measure how much bias is left, because the failed campaigns we see are the visible ones. The official rates we use are averages over all years. Everything we show is a pattern in past campaigns, not a cause. Our test shows which teams get flagged, not how much coaching helps them. And funding is a market test, not proof that a company survives. What would we do next? First, follow live campaigns every day until they end, so that hidden failures get an outcome. Second, test the advice with a real group of teams at Startup at HSG. Third, add other platforms, because some products simply do not fit Kickstarter. We built this with the help of AI assistants, Claude and ChatGPT, which we cite in our repository. Crowdfund Compass does not tell founders they will succeed. It tells a coach where to spend the next hour. Thank you.
